sections.heading: C — Alcohol, drugs and impaired-driving consequences
sections.markdown:
## C — Alcohol, drugs and impaired-driving consequences

FACT_ID: sec16-F01 | anchor: A128
Do not rely on personal or friends' judgments of driving ability after drinking; impairment can occur before visible signs appear. [A128]
Source: [A128 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0128]

FACT_ID: sec16-F02 | anchor: A129
The handbook describes alcohol moving from the stomach and small intestine into the blood and throughout the body. [A129]
Source: [A129 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0129]

FACT_ID: sec16-F03 | anchor: A129
Food in the stomach slows the described absorption compared with an empty stomach; it does not establish safe driving after drinking. [A129]
Source: [A129 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0129]

FACT_ID: sec16-F04 | anchor: A129
Alcohol can dull judgment, inhibition and self-control and impair reaction, coordination, balance, vision and distance judgment. [A129]
Source: [A129 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0129]

FACT_ID: sec16-F05 | anchor: A129
Once alcohol is in the blood, aspirin, coffee, breathing exercises, a slap, physical exercise or food do not sober a person; the source identifies time as the recovery factor. [A129]
Source: [A129 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0129]

FACT_ID: sec16-F06 | anchor: A129
Alcohol can change mood and create false confidence while slowing thinking and reaction. [A129]
Source: [A129 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0129]

FACT_ID: sec16-F07 | anchor: A130
The handbook lists excessive speed, weaving, unusually slow travel, jerky controls and abrupt stops as possible signs of an impaired driver. [A130]
Source: [A130 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec16-F08 | anchor: A130
The source's open-container summary prohibits both the driver and passengers from drinking alcohol or possessing an open alcoholic-beverage container in a vehicle. [A130]
Source: [A130 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec16-F09 | anchor: A130
For the described transport of unsealed alcohol, the handbook directs using the trunk or, if there is no trunk, a position behind the rearmost upright seat. [A130]
Source: [A130 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec16-F10 | anchor: A130
Avoid driving while affected by a drug that could interfere with safe vehicle operation. [A130]
Source: [A130 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec16-F11 | anchor: A130
Combining alcohol with certain medications or drugs can increase impairment and interfere with driving tasks. [A130]
Source: [A130 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec16-F12 | anchor: A130
Ask the prescribing clinician whether a medicine causes drowsiness or otherwise affects driving; if it does, arrange another driver while taking it. [A130]
Source: [A130 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec16-F13 | anchor: A130
Read nonprescription medicine labels and do not drive when the instructions discourage it. [A130]
Source: [A130 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec16-F14 | anchor: A131
The handbook describes drug-impaired driving as being under the influence of either legal or illegal substances. [A131]
Source: [A131 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec16-F15 | anchor: A131
The source describes marijuana as slowing reactions and impairing time and distance judgment. [A131]
Source: [A131 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec16-F16 | anchor: A131
The source associates methamphetamine and cocaine with aggressive or reckless behavior. [A131]
Source: [A131 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec16-F17 | anchor: A131
The source describes opioids as causing drowsiness and affecting memory or thinking, and sedatives as causing dizziness or drowsiness. [A131]
Source: [A131 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec16-F18 | anchor: A131
Impairment-prevention strategies include choosing a designated driver, having that driver keep the keys and arranging rides to and from gatherings involving alcohol or drugs. [A131]
Source: [A131 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec16-F19 | anchor: A131
Other source prevention strategies are avoiding drug-and-alcohol parties and discussing impaired-driving risks with friends. [A131]
Source: [A131 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec16-F20 | anchor: A131
The handbook's under-twenty-one DUI BAC threshold is zero point zero two or higher. [A131]
Source: [A131 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec16-F21 | anchor: A131
For the noncommercial driver aged twenty-one or older, the handbook's DUI BAC threshold is zero point zero eight or higher. [A131]
Source: [A131 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec16-F22 | anchor: A131
The source states that a concentration of zero point twenty or more carries increased penalties. [A131]
Source: [A131 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec16-F23 | anchor: A131
A BAC below zero point zero eight does not preclude a DUI conviction involving other intoxicating substances. [A131]
Source: [A131 -> src:rdmv-id-d:idaho-transportation-department-division:handbook:pdf-0131]

Misconceptions: Coffee and food do not reverse alcohol already in the blood. Legal medications can impair driving. A numerical BAC boundary is not a guarantee of safe driving below it.
Mnemonic: Plan sober transport before the trip is a teaching cue for the supported prevention choices.
Glossary: BAC means blood-alcohol concentration; a designated driver provides sober transport; an SR-twenty-two is the source-named insurance certificate of financial responsibility.
Dynamic facts: legal consequences, medication suitability and insurance compliance require current authoritative review; the handbook is a frozen source description.

verification_debt.claim_text: Physical page one hundred twenty-nine compares one-and-a-half ounces of eighty-proof spirits, five ounces of wine and twelve ounces of beer, then says about an ounce of alcohol each. Wine and beer strengths are unspecified and the alcohol-unit statement needs clinical/source verification. The equivalence and ounce conversion are withheld rather than reproduced as a fact.

The source's alcohol metabolism, sobriety and substance-effect descriptions have not passed the reserved clinical review. No personal dose, elapsed-time-to-sober estimate or medication recommendation is supplied. Release of the clinical content remains blocked.

BAC thresholds, open-container scope, DUI sanctions and traffic-stop legal consequences are source descriptions only. Current statutes, exceptions and amendments have not completed the reserved legal review, so no current-law release is claimed.

Physical pages one hundred twenty-eight and one hundred twenty-nine give BAC-related crash-risk multipliers, beer-arrest share and alcohol/anger crash assertions without dated methods or populations. These statistics are withheld.
The two-through-four-drink impairment onset statement on physical page one hundred twenty-nine lacks individual, dose and time conditions. It is not taught as a threshold below which driving is safe.

Physical page one hundred thirty summarizes an open-container prohibition and trunk/rear storage without enumerating vehicle or statutory exceptions. Source wording is retained, but universal legal applicability requires the legal review.
